fact: CSU's PlantTalk describes xeriscape as planning, improving the soil, choosing suitable plants, and watering, mulching and maintaining well, and names water-conserving grasses such as buffalograss and blue grama as part of it, with mulched areas, decks and paths as alternatives to grass.
quote: By applying the principles of xeriscape, a landscape can be beautiful and diverse while using less water. Planning a landscape, improving the soil, choosing appropriate plants, and proper watering, mulching and maintenance all play a role in conserving water. … Choose water conserving types of grass, such as buffalo or blue grama. Mulched areas, decks and paths are alternatives to grass. … Xeriscapes are low maintenance but do require some care.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1901, Xeriscape Basics

fact: CSU Extension's xeriscape retrofit fact sheet says children's play areas and pet exercise areas are often left in turfgrass that can take heavy wear, and that strips of grass narrower than 8 feet are hard to water with spray heads and can be turned into xeric plantings or hardscape.
quote: Play areas for children and exercise areas for pets are often best left in turfgrasses that can take heavy wear. … Strips of grass narrower than 8 feet are difficult to irrigate effectively with spray heads. Size turf and garden areas accordingly. Irregularly shaped areas should be re-shaped to fit sprinkler irrigation patterns, and the odd-shaped areas converted to appropriately irrigated (or unirrigated) xeric plantings or hardscape.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.234, Xeriscaping: Retrofit Your Yard
notes: Read with curl 2026-09-25. The old URL (extension.colostate.edu/topic-areas/yard-garden/xeriscaping-retrofit-your-yard-7-234/) now redirects to a topics index; this is the fact sheet's current address. CSU means living turfgrass here, not artificial turf: the page may say only that CSU keeps play and pet areas off planted beds.

fact: CSU Extension says some favorite perennials use as much water as a lawn or more, that even drought-tolerant plants need regular, relatively high amounts of water after planting until they establish, which can take days to years depending on plant size, and that water availability should decide when a yard is converted.
quote: Some perennial garden favorites can use as much (or more) water than a lawn. … Note that even drought-tolerant plants require regular and relatively high amounts of water after transplanting or seeding until established. Depending on the size of plant you choose to install in your new xeriscape, this can range from days to years. In general, the smaller the plant the more quickly it establishes. Only after xeric plants are well established can they be gradually weaned from supplemental water. Consider water availability when deciding the timing of a change from a moderate- or high- water use landscape to a xeriscape.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.234, Xeriscaping: Retrofit Your Yard

fact: CSU Extension says weed barrier fabric is not needed under any xeriscape mulch because it restricts water and air reaching the soil and does not prevent weeds in permanent plantings, and that new xeriscapes need regular maintenance to stay weed-free.
quote: Whichever mulch you choose, you do not need to apply weed barrier fabric beneath it—weed fabrics can inhibit water- and air-exchange into the soil and do not actually prevent weed growth in permanent plantings. … New xeriscapes, like any new garden, require maintenance to keep them weed-free and growing.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.234, Xeriscaping: Retrofit Your Yard
notes: PlantTalk 1905 (an older, shorter script) allows a permeable fabric "if an additional weed barrier is needed"; the fact sheet and GardenNotes #245 say to skip it. The page follows the fact sheet.

fact: CSU's PlantTalk says organic mulches such as wood chips break down and need renewing, stone mulches last longer, about 3 inches of mulch controls weeds, and stone mulches store and radiate heat, so large areas of unshaded rock should not go next to a house.
quote: Organic mulches gradually break down and add nutrients to the soil. They will need to be renewed periodically. … Inorganic mulches are stone-based and include rock, cobblestone, pea gravel, lava rock and crushed rock. They last longer than organic mulches and give landscapes a more formal look. Apply about 3” of mulch for weed control. Use less directly around the plants to allow water to reach the root area. Inorganic mulches also store and radiate heat, so avoid putting large areas of unshaded rock next to a house.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1905, Xeriscape Mulches
notes: The heat sentence is also pea-gravel-vs-turf-dog-run.csu-planttalk-rock-heat; this record carries the wider passage this page uses.

fact: CSU Extension says gravel mulch passes more heat into the soil than wood chips and can pass heat to buildings and utilities, that the sunny surface of wood mulch can run hotter than gravel, and that gravel-mulched planting beds stay cooler on the surface than pavement.
quote: Additionally, surface temperatures in planting beds mulched with gravel remain cooler than paved surfaces or surfaces mulched with wood chips. … Gravel mulch transfers more heat to underlying soil than wood chip mulch. This may serve to keep landscape plants in better overall health in cold-winter temperate climates like ours. On the other hand, it can also transfer heat to buildings and utilities or cause some tender plants to begin growing too early in the spring. Wood chip mulch insulates the soil against temperature swings, but the surface temperature of sun-exposed wood mulch can be hotter than that of gravel mulch. Match your mulch to your situation.

fact: CSU Extension says wood chips in Colorado's intense sun can turn water-repellent, so it does not recommend them for xeriscapes unless they are checked and spread often (chips under a leaf canopy or in regularly watered beds are typically not affected), that they can blow away in persistent wind, that stone works as mulch only below about half an inch across, and that mulch should be four inches deep to suppress weeds.
quote: An important consideration for wood chip and bark mulch stems from the intense sunlight and typically dry conditions across much of Colorado. Wood chips exposed to high surface temperatures from intense sunlight can become hydrophobic, preventing water infiltration to the soil. Wood chip or bark mulch, therefore, is not recommended for use in xeriscapes or with open planting plants unless it can be frequently checked and distributed to maintain its ability to conduct water to the soil. Wood chips under a canopy of leaves or in regularly irrigated settings are typically not affected by hydrophobicity. … Wood chips or bark mulch can be less effective in areas with persistent winds, as even relatively large pieces can be blown away in gusty conditions. … Any stones used for mulch should be smaller than a half-inch in diameter for the benefits of water conservation and weed suppression. Larger stone sizes do not function well as mulches and can actually inhibit plant growth but may provide landscape interest. … In order to suppress weed growth, wood chip, gravel, grass clipping, and other mulch should be four inches deep.

fact: CSU's PlantTalk says watering a xeriscape can be cut back after one or two years once transplants establish, and that mulch holds weeds down at first until maturing plants cover the soil and shade them out.
quote: Watering can be reduced after one or two years when transplanted plants are established. Less water applied to mature xeriscapes results in fewer weeds and reduced maintenance. Mulch initially covers the ground minimizing weed growth, and when plants begin to mature, their growth covers the soil leaving little light to promote weed growth.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1910, Xeriscape Maintenance

fact: CSU Extension says drought-tolerant plants are not drought tolerant until their roots establish, that new flowers may need water daily for their first two weeks, that Colorado's common clay soils can stay waterlogged under a dry-looking surface, and that residents should check their water provider's current rules.
quote: Always check with your local water provider for the latest drought information and water use rules and regulations. … Drought tolerant plants are not drought tolerant until their roots are established in the soil. … It is important to assess the moisture in the soil because clay soils, which are common to Colorado, hold moisture for long periods of time after they become water saturated. Although the surface of a clay soil may appear dry and brittle, beneath the surface the soil may be waterlogged and deficient in oxygen needed for plant root growth. … Newly planted flowers may need water daily for the first two weeks following the planting date.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.240, Watering a Home Landscape During Drought

fact: The U.S. EPA says trees and vegetation such as shrubs and tall grasses lower surface and air temperatures by shading the ground and through evapotranspiration, and give habitat and food to pollinating insects.
quote: Trees and vegetation (e.g., bushes, shrubs, tall grasses) lower surface and air temperatures by providing shade and cooling through evapotranspiration. Evapotranspiration is a process in which trees and vegetation absorb water through their roots and evaporate it through their leaves. … Trees and vegetation provide essential habitat and food for many species, including pollinating insects, migratory birds, and small mammals (e.g., bats, squirrels).
source_label: U.S. EPA, Heat Islands: Benefits of Trees and Vegetation
notes: Page last updated December 9, 2025. General heat-island guidance, not a Northern Colorado measurement.

fact: CSU Extension says a planting meant to feed pollinators needs a mix of species blooming from early spring to late fall, and that home gardens can be refuges for pollinators foraging through lawns that lack flowers.
quote: If a habitat is intentionally planted to provide nutrition for pollinators, then it needs to contain a mixture of plant species so that bloom times range from early spring to late fall. This ensures that flowers will be available throughout the pollinator activity season. Home gardens, parks, community gardens, prairies and meadows can all provide pollen and nectar. These habitats can be refuges for pollinators foraging through lawns and farmlands that may not have the floral resources they need.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 5.616, Creating Pollinator Habitat

fact: CSU's PlantTalk says heavy Front Range snow is welcome moisture that lessens the need for winter watering, and that small shrubs flattened by piles of snow may need corrective pruning and can look worse for a couple of years.
quote: When we have heavy snowfalls along the Front Range, it is certainly welcome for the moisture it provides and creates less need to emphasize winter watering. … Small shrubs that are flattened by piles of snow may also need some corrective pruning to remove bent or broken branches. They may have a less-attractive appearance for a couple years.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1754, Snow Impacts on Woody and Herbaceous Plants

fact: CSU Extension says granular magnesium chloride de-icer is commonly spread on sidewalks, driveways and walkways, that magnesium chloride products move from treated roads into nearby soil with precipitation, and that woody plants take up the chloride, which first shows as burned leaf edges and needle tips.
quote: Granulated MgCl2 is also commonly applied to sidewalks, driveways, and walkways in smaller quantities. … MgCl2 based products can move from treated roads into adjacent soils through precipitation. Trees take up soil magnesium and chloride through roots and accumulate them in leaves. … In woody plants, chloride toxicity typically first appears as marginal necrosis on the leaves of deciduous species (Figure 1), or as tip burn and necrosis on the needles of conifers (Figure 2).
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 7.425, Magnesium Chloride Toxicity in Trees
notes: The fact sheet is written about roadside trees; its quick facts and first section name sidewalks, driveways and walkways as places granular MgCl2 is used. The page says only that plants in a bed along a salted walk are exposed, and cites artificial-turf-snow-removal.fieldturf-deicers for the turf side.
